speakeroldname: Hon. George Hees (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: COMMEMORATION OF SERVICE MEN AND WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my proud duty to remind Members of the House that Canada will be observing Remembrance Day next Monday. Last year I said it was not sufficient to recognize the sacrifices of veterans and their families merely on special occasions. I said they must be regarded as a very special group, worthy of our unsparing attention each and every day. I am thankful that we in this House have been able to give a practical expression to those sentiments during the past 12 months.
I would like to thank members of all Parties in the House for so enthusiastically supporting the provision of additional funds for the benefit of many more thousands of veterans and their families. One of the first pieces of legislation passed by the House allowed the Department of Veterans Affairs to streamline and upgrade long established veterans' programs. I am particularly grateful for the advice and co-operation 1 received from all Members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs in the preparation of this legislation.
Canadians have been reminded once again this year of the achievement of the men and women we are serving here in Parliament. Some veterans returned to Sicily and Italy to pay their respects to those Canadians who died during a harsh
20-month campaign fought long before the rest of the Allied Forces arrived in Europe on D-Day. Others of us returned to Holland to be greeted with love as representatives of Canadians who liberated that wonderful country 40 years before. Next month another pilgrimage will be going to Asia. There Canada will be able to salute those who were among the first to see action and the last to see freedom again, the defenders of Hong Kong. Cemeteries in Singapore and Burma will be visited by veterans, including some of our own colleagues, who flew so many dangereous missions in that forgotten theatre.
These pilgrimages are always occasions for both sadness and pride. The rows of Canadian graves and the lists of names on memorials are a terrible reminder of the price our country has had to pay in war. Our pride comes from rediscovering just how much respect our service men and women gained for Canada overseas.
I would like to quote some remarks made by the Dutch Minister of Transport when we Canadians visited Holland last May. She said at that time: "During the war Canada was, in the Dutch peoples' eyes, a big, free, hospitable country far away from the acts of war. During the war it was that country whose sons and daughters were willing to risk their lives, and sometimes sacrifice their lives, for the liberation of Europe. The children from that paradise called Canada wore uniforms and went to a hell called Europe. To us, the Dutch, Canada is still a concept we link with freedom and courage".
Such words, Mr. Speaker, eloquently explain why it will be such a privilege for Canadians to commemorate the two World Wars and the Korean War next Monday.

subtopic: COMMEMORATION OF SERVICE MEN AND WOMEN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, as spokesperson for the Official Opposition, I welcome this opportunity to join the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) in paying tribute to those Canadians whose memory we shall be honouring on Remembrance Day, Monday, November 11.
The Minister referred to the trip to the Netherlands made by our veterans early this year to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the end of hostilities of the Second World War.
I am sure all Canadians were very proud and very moved by the many stories about this visit that were published in the media. On television, we also saw the joy, love and pride with which thousands of Dutch people welcomed our veterans back to their country.
Personally, I was very impressed to see so many young children waving Canadian flags. They seemed to be very much

November 8, 1985
Remembrance Day
aware, and at the same time grateful to all those Canadian veterans who were proudly parading past them.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that today's youth in Canada will also show this gratitude to our Canadian veterans.
Since 1953, Canada has not engaged in any armed conflict. If our young people wonder why Canada celebrates Remembrance Day, they should remember the supreme sacrifice made by generations that went before, to give them a present so few had been able to enjoy for so long: peace and freedom.
We enjoy the unusual privilege of peace. Freedom is an integral part of our daily lives in this country. On Remembrance Day, we shall pay tribute to the suffering and bloodshed with which others paid for this freedom.
There is also fear, the fear felt by those who went overseas and who had to face the enemy, and the fear of those who stayed home, waiting anxiously until a telegram announced that a relative or a friend was wounded or killed in battle.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are not demonstrative people. Remembrance Day has never lost its sacred characteristic, nor its silent dignity, nor its link with past events. The Flanders poppy is a discreet reminder of World War I atrocities and sacrifices-over 67 years ago already.
Speaking of the poppy, I would remind the House that the Royal Canadian Legion is celebrating its 60th anniversary this year. The Legion has been the staunch defender of veterans' rights and the protector of their families for the last 60 years. I commend the Legion for past achievements and I fully expect its future endeavours to be equally illustrious.
As parades worm their way through Canadian cities on Monday, bagpipers will remind us of our grief, buglers will blow the last post. But we will not highlight Remembrance Day by displays of new missiles, fly-pasts, or tanks thundering down the streets. We do have such weapons, of course, but that is not what Remembrance Day means to Canadians. We can still appreciate what Remembrance Day represents-an opportunity to recall Canadian men and women who made the ultimate sacrifice so we may live as we do today, free!
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, allow me to read a verse from a poem written by John McCrae, physician, poet and soldier, entitled "Somewhere in Flanders":
You who survive us, it is up to you to take the torch of combat from our emaciated fingers, it is a sacred duty, we shall not sleep under the soil of Flanders if you desecrate it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over 70 years have passed since the first Canadian died overseas in the fight for freedom against totalitarianism. This year marks the fortieth anniversary of the end of the Second World War, a war which I lived through in Britain as a child and which my father, together with so many other fathers of other young
men and boys and girls, the brothers and the sisters and the cousins and the other relatives, took part. I remember that at the end of that war we vowed it would never happen again and that we would, in fact, remember the sacrifices. We vowed that we would remember those who died and that we would, in a more tangible way, recognize the sacrifice of those who returned from that war wounded, in body and, in some instances, in mind. I ask the House to think back about whether in fact we have lived up to that obligation, to that undertaking to which we committed ourselves at that time without a moment's hesitation.
In 1984 1 had the privilege of travelling with hundreds of veterans as they returned to the places which are indelibly inscribed in their memories. I stood on the shores and at the battle scenes and heard of the terror, the sacrifice and the bravery first hand. I met, with others from Canada, those in France who had befriended and protected our men as they fought for freedom.
I knew then what Remembrance Day was all about and why we, who benefited from the sacrifice, committed ourselves to ensuring that this could never happen again. We continue to owe a great deal to those whose lifetime was one of great sacrifice and suffering, to the widows and families of those who lost their lives.
On behalf of my colleagues, I want to join with the Minister and the representative of the Liberal Party in paying tribute and rededicating ourselves now to meeting our debt to those who served our country, who served it in World War I and World War II, to those who served in the Korean conflict and to those who continue to serve in the many peacekeeping missions in which we take part around the world as part of our obligation.
I continue to pray that we will not lose sight, as Parliament, of the need to develop an economic order throughout the world which will eliminate poverty and want and establish for all people a sense of belonging that will guarantee the level of life-style that will, by its very existence, put an end to the threat of war.

Mr. Speaker, we remember.

SITUATION IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Tory federal Government in the name of deficit reduction is cutting back on family benefits, on social programs, on transfer payments to provinces for health and education, and on essential public service jobs. While professing to care about those in greatest need, it is copying the B.C. policy of restraint which has made a devastating contribution to unemployment, poverty, and human rights.
Bill Bennett in British Columbia cut social service programs, eliminated child protection teams, family support workers, closed the Rentalman's office, disbanded the Human Rights Commission, laid off consumer protection officers, closed transition houses and fired elected schoolboards.
While unemployment remains at 14.2 per cent, the third highest in Canada, the number of poor families in B.C. has increased by 400 per cent since 1980. A 400 per cent increase in poverty is a crisis, Mr. Speaker. The federal Government by adding another layer of restraint will add to the poverty and hardship of British Columbians and other Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, this week has been designated as Crime Prevention Week in Canada, with the theme being victims. I wish to take this opportunity to address the House on the importance of this issue.
Violence is always tragic, but none so tragic as that violence which occurs within the family. Abuse of children and wife battering are far more widespread than most Canadians imagine. For example, it has been estimated that at least one in 10 Canadian wives is beaten by her husband in any given year.
There are transition houses and crisis centres for victims which provide an invaluable service for abused children and battered wives. However, they are too few and underfunded. Such a centre exists in my riding in Manitoba, the Dauphin Crisis Centre for Battered Women and Abused Children. The dedicated people involved in this Centre offer counselling, referrals, general information and, in the near future, hope to provide short-term emergency shelter.
The Government has promised that, in consultation with the provinces, it will take action to provide additional assistance to the victims of family violence. It can never be too soon to provide the victims of family violence with somewhere to turn. They need and deserve the support of this House, the provincial Governments, and all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

ANNOUNCEMENT OF FACTORY FREEZER TRAWLER LICENCES- EFFECT ON NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a sad day for the fishery and for politics in Newfoundland. The federal Government has announced not just one factory freezer trawler licence, but it has offered two more factory freezer trawler licences, one of them to a provincial-federal Crown corporation, namely, Fishery Products International, which licence was not even requested.
We have the sad situation today in Newfoundland of having the federal Government calling the provincial Government names and the provincial Government calling the federal Government names in open battle. I think that is pretty sad, Mr. Speaker, and is a bad reflection on our political system. What it requires is a full hearing on the matter as far as factory freezer trawlers versus the inshore fishermen are concerned, and for everybody to keep in mind that the best quality of fish is that caught by the inshore fishermen in a trap or by hook and line.
I am hoping that the provincial Government and the federal Government can resolve these differences, because it certainly does nobody any good when we have this situation occurring in a Province like Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise today to address an issue of concern expressed to me on numerous occasions. The complaint is that changes to the 1978 firearms control law adversely affect the ownership and use of recreational firearms.
Several reports and evaluations commissioned by the House have indicated that the 1978 changes had little impact on firearms crime. Instead, the resulting growth of the bureaucracy has increased costs, with questionable results.

Mr. Speaker, this House must take into consideration requests for the revision and simplification of that law. Recreational firearms can be controlled much more cheaply and effectively.
Firearms control authorities are primarily police officers. Their view of recreational firearms is rightly constrained by their training and experience, but this can lead to unnecessary friction between honest citizens who use firearms for recreational purposes and the authorities.
The diversity of firearms disciplines makes it difficult to achieve adequate control of the use of recreational firearms without enlisting the co-operation of the community itself, which we have not done.
Our present firearms registration system is deficient. A new system, devised jointly by the authorities and the recreational firearms community, would be cheaper and more effective. This is an area where co-operation between citizens and Government could be improved. On behalf of the recreational firearms community in my constituency, I call for a review of the firearms control laws, with the full participation of representatives of that community.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DEATH OF UKRAINIAN POET, VASYL STUS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have followed the case of Vasyl Stus very closely. All Members of this House are deeply saddened by his death. The House may recall that five or six months ago, when I was in the Ukraine, I had the opportunity to raise directly with the leaders of the Government of the Ukraine the deep concern of Canada about the human rights situation in the Ukraine and elsewhere in the Soviet Union. We intend to continue to make that kind of representation on behalf of human rights everywhere in the world, but particularly behind the Iron Curtain. Member's suggestion under advisement as well.

It is a rather important point of order, as you will undoubtedly realize and so recognized at the time. This, of course, is the first opportunity we have had to bring this matter to the attention of the House because under our generally accepted proceedings it is not possible at the time of adjournment to bring up points of order. Member for Kamloops-Shus-wap (Mr. Riis), pursuant to Standing Order 30, moved that the House do adjourn. It came about that the bells were made to ring on that issue in order to bring in the Members to vote thereon.

We mentioned three of them here: (1) to develop new job potential in Quebec communities; (2) to ease the tax burden on low and middle income families; and (3) to protect and safeguard key existing industries in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, 1 suppose you remember the election on September 4, 1984 very well. It was certainly a great victory for the Progressive Conservative Party across Canada, including the province of Quebec. It was an overwhelming victory.
After 21 years with the Liberal Party in power, the people of Canada and Quebec voted for a change, and the Progressive Conservative Party won 211 seats across this country, including 58 in the province of Quebec.
However, Mr. Speaker, the situation has changed, and it did so very quickly. Canadians are very disappointed. The turnaround took place in the last two or three months, and according to the last Gallup Poll, the Progressive Conservative Party dropped from 50 per cent to 45 per cent of the popular vote across Canada, while the Opposition parties, the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party, made a 10 per cent gain.
According to the latest Crop poll in Quebec, Mr. Speaker, where the Progressive Conservative Party came out with a huge majority some 13 or 14 months ago, that Party now ranks second and the New Democratic Party is third with 22 per cent of the votes.
November 8, 1985

Mr. Speaker, it proves that people in Quebec and the other provinces are disenchanted with the Government team across the aisle. Why this change, Mr. Speaker? Why such changes in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada after only 13 months?
First, the image of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). He is not competent at all, he is badly organized, and then the question did arise as to whether the Prime Minister had told the House of Commons the whole truth about the tuna incident.
Second, two Ministers had to resign, the former Minister of Communications and the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
More significant still, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister broke the election promises he had made to men and women in Quebec and in the rest of Canada.
During the 1984 summer election campaign the Prime Minister and his Party made hundreds of promises, but Canadians can see now that the promises are not being honoured.
First of all, the Prime Minister made an election promise respecting employment. What he said was: "Jobs, jobs, jobs". So where do we stand after one year? Statistics Canada made their figures public this morning, and the unemployment rate is now 10.3 per cent in Canada, and this is the seasonally adjusted rate, Mr. Speaker. Our unemployment rate is 10.3 per cent, but the United States reported a rate of only 7.1 per cent in October, while the number of unemployed in Sweden and Japan is roughly 3 per cent. In October last year 1,305,000 Canadians were without jobs, yet in October this year 1,200,000 Canadians were still looking for work. That is only a difference of 105,000 fewer unemployed for the 13 months the Progressive Conservative Party has been in power, in spite of the fact that the recession in the world has nearly come to an end, that interest rates all over the world are lower now than a year ago, and that oil prices are now lower than a year ago. There are still in Canada 1,200,000 unemployed people, which represents an unemployment rate of 10.3 per cent.
In the province of Quebec, the unemployment situation is pretty bad, especially in Montreal East, Desbiens and Valley-field. The unemployment rate in the province reached 11.8 per cent last month, and between September and October, 8,000 people lost their jobs in the transportation industry. In the trade and commerce industry, there were 10,000 more unemployed people than the previous month. What sort of future do you think the young people who are unemployed have in the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker? The Prime Minister has broken his promise to create jobs for Canadian men and women in Quebec and everywhere else in Canada.

Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) mentioned it two or three times, that Mr. Trudeau's Government limited the amount of family allowances at the time of the 6 and 5 per cent, when we had inflation rates of 15, 16, 17 and 18 per cent, that the increase in family allowances was restricted to those 5 and 6 per cent. It is strictly the same thing, Mr. Speaker.
In conclusion, what we need in this country is a real change, what we need is a Government for ordinary citizens. We are an immensely wealthy country. We have a positive people facing our future. We have vast quantities of natural resources, but let us not forget what happened in other countries of the world, for instance in France, in Germany and in Japan. All three countries were almost completely destroyed during the Second World War forty years ago. Now, the standard of living in France, in Germany and in Japan is almost the same as ours. Mr. Speaker, why in a country such as Sweden having a population almost the same as that in Quebec, the unemployment rate is between 2 or 3 per cent? Why is the standard of living as high in that country as in Canada?

And I frankly believe that no Hon. Member in this House can deny it.
The Prime Minister of Canada is blamed for not having kept his promises. In fact he has four years to do so. Thousands of jobs have been lost in both these industries.
And my hon. friends know it. I am not putting the blame especially on the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) for that. I am not saying anything of the sort, Mr. Speaker. What I am saying is that before blaming us for jobs which are being lost in a difficult climate which is not of our own making, Mr. Speaker-
One should be careful before accusing this new Government which is striving every day to repair the almost irreparable, Mr. Speaker. That is what we are up against. There is more. For instance, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) blamed us for the billion-dollar rescue of the banks, as if we had wished those people or any bank in Canada to experience such difficulties. That is not true, Mr. Speaker. We have to deal with the situation. We try to make the best of it and I think we have shown the best of dispositions toward those who put their confidence and their money in those banks. Then again, we will be told that we only protect the rich because we reacted, we realized the importance of suppressing any doubt about the credibility of our banking institutions. We had no other choice. We had to act, and we did. 1 know that action will prove to be quite worthwhile, in the mean and long term, Mr. Speaker, because we cannot afford to leave any doubt about the credibility of our banking institution and jeopardize the investments we need from abroad and within Canada. So we responded to a situation we inherited, Mr. Speaker.
I do not want to spend all the time I have critizing our predecessors, but I say we have changed course in the last fourteen months. As our colleagues of the opposition know, because the figures are there to prove it, the economic conditions are more favourable, and business people have a greater degree of confidence. Of course, this morning mention was made of a slight increase in the unemployment figure but people seem to forget, for example, that over the last 12 months, more than 300,000 jobs were created in Canada and nearly 100,000 of those were in Quebec; the matter came up no doubt as a result of the poll published this morning, and 1 am not happy with these figures, Mr. Speaker, of course I am not. But the question is: so we really want to see our economy take an upward trend and get our country back on the road to prosperity? That is the question we have to ask ourselves, and each and every Member in this House is moraly responsible for achieving that goal which is not only to have our country regain its economic stature, but also to have a sound economy.
1 think every member, in the Opposition as in the Government, has a certain responsibility towards this objective and I think that we ought not to go beyond what is generally accepted. To level criticisims is very easy, Mr. Speaker, and I have
been in the ranks of the Opposition before, but never have I indulged in petty politics. 1 did not want to be considered as a second-rate politician, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I have consistently refused to score political points at the expense of the elderly, as was done here recently when it was implied that our party is against the poor and the elderly. God knows, Mr. Speaker, we have a lot of respect for these people, and if we work so hard to get our economy going again it is especially in the interests of the poor and the elderly, Mr. Speaker! Some will say that our investment oriented policies are directed only at those who are capable of investing. Of course, they are! Mr. Speaker, farmers, businessmen and homeowners are fully aware of the impact of the $500,000 maximum capital gains tax exemption. But why did we abolish the capital gains tax! To give people an incentive to re-invest in their own country- they are free to do so and we have confidence in Canadians- and also to create jobs so that we will be able to give work to those who are unfortunate enough to depend on unemployment insurance or who for too long have been living off welfare.
It is part of an over-all strategy, Mr. Speaker, and those people know it. I would suggest that the initiatives we have taken will pave the way to economic recovery, particularly certain agreements we have signed with Quebec. I am proud of them, so are all my Quebec colleagues, and I commend them. However, Mr. Speaker, I remain somewhat wary of the Opposition approach. I keep wondering whether they really want us to succeed in getting the economy back on the right track and creating new jobs.
You know, the previous Government has institutionalized unemployment. I have to point out that the number of unemployed went from 300,000 or 400,000 to 1,750,000 in the last
12	or 13 years. They probably think we are biting off more than we can chew when we say we want to reverse this trend, but they should help us anyway. They should react positively, and I will be the first to applaud if they can recommend incentive measures to create jobs. But they refuse to support our efforts to achieve that goal, however noble it may be since that is how we want to give renewed hopes to our youths and make elderly Canadians feel even more secure. No wonder I entertain serious misgivings about the objectivity of those people who are launching unrelenting attacks against us barely
13	or 14 months after we took office.
Mr. Speaker, over the last 14 months we have steered a different course so as to expect better days. The economic picture is brighter: interest rates are lower, as I said earlier and the number of bankruptcies has also decreased significantly; we have evidence that confidence in the economy is growing and that negociations on tremendously important projects are about to start. With regard to our negotiations on free trade, there again the Opposition is quick to spread doom and gloom and predict failure while alarming Canadians with dismal predictions. The biggest mistake this Government could make would be not to move with regard to free trade.
November 8, 1985

We are aware that not only must we begin negotiations but we also have to open wide our ears to have meaningful discussions with our American partners, neighbours and allies. We are aware of the challenge and the work involved. But doing nothing would be irresponsible from this Government and we are not irresponsible people, so we shall tackle those negotiations face to face with a very specific goal in mind: to improve what we have and to increase the number of jobs directly related to our export markets. That is our goal, Mr. Speaker, and we think that we will therefore entirely fulfill the responsibilities given to us.
I might add that as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, I was also very happy to agree to a payment of $27 million to compensate farmers following crop losses they suffered in 1983. We have not found it necessary to refund those people. It has now been done, Mr. Speaker. We also approved a $26.7 million payment under a crop insurance program. Funds of $16 million have also been earmarked for a very interesting industry in Sainte-Foy, namely an optic and laser centre. And what about the settlement of the Mirabel claims? I think that all the Hon. Members are quite happy with the settlement which I was able to achieve with the expropriated landowners within nine months of being appointed. Naturally, we hope, by implementing relevant policies, to be able to give back to these farm lands their former natural beauty and usefulness.
Mr. Speaker, I know that my allotted time is nearly over, but while this motion accuses us of having forgetten Quebec and of not thinking about the poor, our whole economic policy is aimed at helping those who need it the most. The Opposition can do whatever they like, we shall probably refuse to develop a social policy as a whole. We are honestly and sincerely trying to help those most in need, but we shall have to create a renewed prosperity. Then, we shall be able to provide more assistance to those who need it the most, and, like the Members opposite, we shall be quite happy to improve the lot of those we represent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the comments of the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), and I must say that either his comments are demagogic, or else the Minister is making very valid efforts without receiving any support from his Quebec colleagues.
I have noted his commitment concerning the shoe industry. However, I also remind him that he made the firm commitment during his election campaign that his Government would pay $13 million to hog producers. There is one thing I know, and that is that if the Minister had got his way, this amount of $13 million would have been repaid a long time ago.
Supply
However, I have been wondering, and this is my question: How come he does not get the support of his Quebec caucus, which is quite powerful, for this kind of initiative?
I also have a subordinate question. The previous Government had made commitments which were endorsed by the conservatives during the election campaign, namely, the cartography project and the agricultural laboratory in Victoria-ville-where, I believe, he is going this weekend-which was to specialize in plant diseases and protection. They also promised to build a gas pipeline between Sherbrooke, Windsor and Asbestos. These were firm commitments. Why didn't he deliver? Why didn't he carry out such projects which would have created much employment?

Mr. Speaker, I shall not go back to 1979, when our friends opposite defeated us over an 18 cents a gallon tax. We know what happened afterwards.
So I would have lots to say about honesty.
As concerns the $13 million that were promised to hog producers, I remember having promised $27 million during the election campaign for crop losses. A $30 million figure was mentioned but we settled for $27 million. That amount was paid by our Government.
The Hon. Member mentioned a $13 million commitment, but he forgets, once again, to mention and thank me for the $27 million which was given to farmers in his constituency and elsewhere in Canada. He forgets about it, but that is understandable.
As for the $13 million intended for hog producers, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows perfectly well that we could have settled that question soon after the election, if it had not been for the position our American neighbours have taken about that industry. He understands it so well, Mr. Speaker, that he could even explain the situation to me. We were actually embarrassed, because we feared that a quick payment of that subsidy might have resulted in the loss of export markets as high as 25 per cent for hog producers in Quebec. That would not have been very helpful so soon after the election.
He mentions several other projects, such as the Cartographic Centre which, obviously, he should know is still alive. However, the Hon. Member will understand that we have a $200 billion deficit, the legacy of these gentlemen of the previous Government who forgot to take care of that before they left. So we have a small debt of just $200 billion, the servicing of which costs some $25 billion. Obviously, we had to postpone certain projects because of that, not only in Quebec but all over Canada.
Heaven knows, Mr. Speaker, how much I would like to carry out these projects as Minister of Public Works. That would really make me happy. Due to various considerations

November 8, 1985
Supply
and budgetary restraints, it has not been possible to go ahead, but we have not forgetten or rejected these projects.
It is our hope, Mr. Speaker, that as we proceed with this economic recovery, we can implement those projects as soon as possible, both in the area of cartography and others, in the best interests of all Quebecers, and in all the constituencies of Quebec.
There is no problem about that, Mr. Speaker, and it is not always easy, as the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe very well knows. He did not mention the footwear industry in his remarks to me, because he knows perfectly well, having been a Member of a Government which unfortunately had problems with the footwear industry, yes, he knows perfectly well that this cannot be solved as easily as he would hope, and if it was that easy, I wonder why he did not do so during the eight or ten years he was with the Government, and a majority Government besides.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) for his liveliness, the way he defends the interests not only of Quebec but of Canada, and of this country's economic situation.
I would like to congratulate him no just for the work he is doing in this House, but also because he is a most able Minister.
I have a question for him. He mentioned an investment in Edmonton. Could he give a few details on what is being done with respect to that investment?

Mr. Speaker, true enough, this may not be the most difficult question, however, it is relevant.
I assume that each one of you would like to have a project that would be creating 2,000 jobs over the next three years. In the larger National Capital region, here in Ottawa, we have no cause for complaint, there are museums that are proceeding well, and so on. So in the case of Edmonton, it is a major federal presence that will be called Place Canada, in Edmonton proper where a hotel, office, and business complex will be built, of course, for the benefit of people living in Edmonton. And, there is not doubt about it, the federal Government probably will also have congenial office space for its public servants in Edmonton.
What to my mind was the most interesting for Edmonton, considering the unemployment rate in the construction industry prevailing in the great City of Edmonton, in that great region of Canada, since there were economic problems there as elsewhere, I think, was this compensation, this federal presence which responded to a need in the construction industry. I remember quite well that the unions at that time had talked to me about that as well as other people concerned, civic authorities and the Members of this House. Our Members, Mr. Speaker, had told me that it would be relevant to have a major project there because of the economic circumstances existing in Edmonton.
As a Quebecer and as Minister of Public Works, I will admit, Mr. Speaker, in this fine spirit of national reconciliation, that I was proud last Tuesday to dedicate this first-rate complex which will take shape during the forthcoming months, of course to the great satisfaction of Westerners.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the previous speaker.
Mr. Speaker, on May 4, 1984, in the Sherbrooke newspaper La Tribune, the following could be read: "A Tory Government would not remove quotas on imports set by Canada in the footwear and textile industries as indicated Wednesday to La Tribune, by the Conservative Leader Brian Mulroney. The quota policy will remained unchanged, according to Mr. Mulroney who said that he was not in favour of free trade in those areas."

Mr. Speaker, I would like to know whether the Hon. Minister can tell us if the Cabinet remembers the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on May 4, 1984, when he was seeking the votes of footwear workers and others in Quebec. We have heard "delay, delay, delay" in the past two months. The Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) said that there will be an answer, but we have heard that for weeks and weeks. Members have asked when we are going to hear a statement. We know that retailers are not buying from Canadian buyers because they are waiting for the end of the quota in three weeks. When will the statement be made and will it honour the pledge made by the Prime Minister?
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to inform my hon. colleague that a decision will be made before November 30.

speechtext: The period provided for comments has now expired. Debate. The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme).

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Earlier, when I was listening to the Hon. Member who presented the motion for the NDP, and who comes from a riding in Saskatchewan, I felt that I had to tell him, first of all, that I did not have to be grateful to him for presenting this motion and limiting it to Quebec, because in any case, he know and his party knew, that yesterday, today and tomorrow we were having a general meeting in Halifax, where the majority of the Quebec caucus, at least our party's Quebec caucus, since they don't have any Members from Quebec, would probably be attending. At the request of my whip, the person responsible for party discipline, we managed to get some of our Members to stay, because this motion, in addition to condemn-
November 8, 1985

ing the Government, might also be construed as an attempt to demonstrate, at least partly, that the party I represent, which has had many Members from the province of Quebec and which very shortly, I am sure, will be able to win back the trust of Quebecers ... so 1 certainly do not have to be grateful to him for the way he, in a more or less rhetorical fashion, limited his motion, although after listening to him via the television cameras, I had not heard anything that concerned Quebec. He did not speak at all to the motion before the House, the motion concerning Quebec and the fact that this Government has apparently abandoned the province of Quebec.
I thought he was exaggerating a bit, especially when I heard him talking about social programs. Having always been an avid reader of La Fontaine's fables, if I may on this Friday afternoon, Mr. Speaker, and this is quite relevant, 1 should like to relate what came immediately to my mind. When 1 listened to my very good friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) 1 was reminded of another fable. The NDP Members who openly take credit for all social programs reminded me of La Fontaine's fable about the stagecoach and the fly. It is unfortunate that young Quebecers and Francophones in the rest of Canada are no longer taught La Fontaine's fables, everybody should know them because they seem to always apply in every human situation. Now, about the stagecoach and the fly, I will skip the first few lines. It was going uphill on a sandy and tough road which was hard to climb. It goes something like this: "The fly sees horses coming. It gets the idea that buzzing them will help. It stings them one after another, convinced that it alone keeps them pulling the coach. Indeed it takes full merit and complains it is doing all the work. After an arduous climb the coach finally reaches the top of the hill and the fly says: Now I can breathe, I worked so hard for those poor people, they Finally made it to level ground".
My friend the Minister of Public Works takes it for granted that all of a sudden everything is peachy and inflation is going down, as if the previous Government did not have anything to do with that. But it does take time and the downward trend was clearly unmistakable before the elections when the inflation rate was 4 per cent and interest rates were levelling off. There is one of La Fontaine's fables which applies, not to him, but to his Party, the one about the frog trying to grow as big as an ox. This really applies, Mr. Speaker, to the Government which claims all the merit for the completion of almost everyone of the big projects which were already started and for which it just had, as was mentioned yesterday by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) to reap what others have sown.
What strikes me, Mr. Speaker, is that during the debate on this motion today, the Hon. Member of the NDP did not really make any reference to his motion, which will probably allow the Government and Official Opposition Members to digress a
Supply
little, but I will leave to my colleague and friend, the Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif), to speak about the third part of the today's motion, that is:
Protect and safeguard Key existing industries such as lumber, textiles, agriculture, pulp and paper and footwear.
I will entrust my colleague and friend of Richmond-Wolfe to do that.
I was not offended because we are among colleagues, and there is no reason to be shocked because one of then says things he or she might not like, however I was somewhat surprised at the strategy of the NPD which had the whole debate revolue around the situation in Quebec. Obviously, the Gallup Poll gave them temporarily 22 per cent and they believe, of course, they have made extraordinary progress; they imagine themselves in power, as the fly of the la Fontaine fable they see themselves at the top of the hill. Well, 1 must say to him, Mr. Speaker, that I would have liked to see him make the same remarks in English, because what I do not like with the NDP, with socialists-although socialists are very respectable people-I so not mean nasty and mean socialists, but socialists-They always take the same approach to debates in a very clever but around about way, the class struggle approach. I find this dangerous, expecially when they say "The rich get richer and the poor get poorer" I have seen the theme of their campaigns "Let's make the rich pay". It has a demagogic and sad ring to it. It seems to me that there should be a better way to approach this debate, and I say that out of friendship for my colleagues, because when people hear those words and take them at face value they might reach in a violent way which I do not think is what the NDP had is mind the NDP, formerly the CCF and eventually I don't know what-I feel, Mr. Speaker, that one must always guard against this kind of class struggle rhetoric.
Having said that, I of course agree with them when they say the Government has reneged on its commitments. The abandonment mostly of their social programs because, as the Hon. Minister of Public Works said earlier: There are people in the political world who are trying to make us believe that we want to frighten the elderly, the old people, our elders. I would never dare accuse one of my opponents, even if during the last election campaign my opponents travelled across the constituency saying: Mr. Prud'homme is scaring you. I will not repeat what I said when I met those elderly people because of those who know my constituency, there are 12 homes for the elderly, I have known those people forever and they would have kicked me out if I had dared go and stir them up, scare our senior citizens, and as 1 said at the time, almost several months ago, it would have been a shame for my father who died at 90 to hear that his son could have gone to an old citizens home just to stir them up. But it was indeed facts that led us to go and speak to those people. It was facts. And what were those facts? The fact was that the Government decided to de-index old age

November 8, 1985
Supply
pensions. They are saying: Well, no, it was not serious. But 1 ask them: If your intention was not really to de-index and roll back pensions, why did you do it? It was the people's involvement that made you step back. And I have to say that I shall not be claiming the merit of that achievement for my party, and even less so for those who jumped on the bandwagon, the CCF Party which joined us in the wake of the efforts by our colleague, our champion, the one we had chosen within our party to be a leader on those matters, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart).
But at the same time, and for the first time in their lives, the people of Canada got organized. Senior citizens who used to remain silent got their act together.
And I must say that I strongly oppose what I always hear from our socialist friends in Canada, that the Liberal Party also had brought down indexation, had de-indexed with its six and five program . .. which is misleading because that is not what happened. The deindexation proposed by the Government related to the first 3 percent ... it was an immediate attack against senior citizens, those who received those cheques, to remove the first 3 percent saying .. . you will have nothing. However, the temporary proposal of the government at that time, and it did not last very long because inflation decreased rapidly, was 6 percent and 5 percent the following year, and it was not enough. But this hardly occurred because inflation decreased to 6 and 5 percent. Thus there is a difference between taking immediately the first 3 percent and what we did at that time.
It is the same as far as family allowances are concerned. I am very pleased to see that a distinguished colleague, a friend of Hon. Members' who is not a Liberal, an Hon. Member from the east end of Montreal, has just started to realize how dangerous the situation is, because she is now presenting petitions. The day before yesterday, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Mercier (Mrs. Jacques) presented petitions similar to those presented by all my colleagues, asking for the Government to withdraw their Bill on the deindexation of family allowances.
Why all this? Because it is related to the end of my speech. The Hon. Member, if anyone is honourable in this House he is, the former Minister of National Defence and Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), presented a motion on behalf of his constituents to oppose deindexation. He is not a Liberal! He is not a member of the NDP!
He stood up by presenting a petition, and I do not know whether he spoke against the legislation or not, but he presented a petition, which was remarkable, knowing that it would be embarrassing for the Government.
Take it from me, Mr. Speaker: before the debate on the Government's plan to deindex family allowances is over, even my colleague the Hon. Member for Verdun will be tabling petitions calling on the Government to renounce its plan.
Mr. Speaker, the Government has failed to fulfil its promises concerning the well known RRAP-I cannot stand these acronyms!-Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. The activities in Quebec under this program have considerably decreased, while in Ontario they have hardly decreased. I cannot help thinking. I see in the statistics published this morning that Ontario is somewhat better off. There are 7,000 more jobs in Ontario. Unemployment has decreased. But for Quebec and other Eastern Canada regions which are faced with the same problems, it is simply more, much more of the same.
I should like to know what the elected representatives of the ridings I am going to name-I am not going to name all of them-have done about the RRAP-I do not think the hon. member who represents the City of Victoriaville is a Liberal. 1 hear that my friend the Hon. Member for Trois-Riviere was met with a demonstration, and that something resembling a sit-in took place at the PC office. I hear also that Gilbert ... I mean the Hon. Member for Verdun has had his own problems. I can see our good friend the Minister, that is, the Hon. Member for Rimouski-Temiscouata (Mrs. Vezina) who manages to calm us with her smile when the goings get rough. Major cuts were also made in her own riding, and the people there fumed. The elected representatives of East Angus, Becancour, even Victoria . . . The Council of mayors ... A council of Bellechasse mayors say the same thing. A good friend from Rouyn-Noranda. They must be embarrassed. 1 hope they will find some way of explaining the unexplainable. Would you believe, Mr. Speaker, that a colleague who presides over our proceedings as you do, the Hon. Member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Charest), also has problems. Questions are asked in Sherbrooke, in Windsor.
So, Mr. Speaker, those promises must be fulfilled. Those cuts hurt middle-income earners and those who are ill off.
I could go on and on. Broken promises! Lord! I will be charitable and suppose the Government will eventually honour those promises, as the Minister of Public Works who responded on behalf of the Government said earlier. He asked for a chance for a Government that has been in power for only twelve, thirteen or fourteen months. I am quite prepared to give them a chance, since that allowed them to make all overtures. Everything they take credit for would have happened anyway, without them. Personally, and that is the advice I gave my colleagues, I prefer to start applying more pressure on the Government after eighteen months, two years or two years and a half. That is when the Conservative Government will be applying its own policies, which I fear.
In Montreal, as a last word on RRAP, Mr. Marcel Sevigny, the spokesman of demonstrators, was quoted in La Presse of Wednesday, March 20, 1985, as saying: "One hundred and twenty-five representatives of housing co-operatives on the
November 8, 1985

Island of Montreal demonstrated yesterday ..." I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that those people will make the Conservative Government members move. There is no doubt about that.
I can say one thing, and that is my reply to those who say things were bad before. Even though my colleagues in my own party do not agree with my interpretation of our defeat, I believe the Canadian people seemed to have had enough with us. Very well. They made a decision. They re-elected 40 members of our party. I thank them, like my colleagues Rossi, Tardif and others who came back. We thank the people for keeping us but they decided they wanted a change. They decided that the Hon. Member for Rimouski was good enough, that the Hon. Member for Verdun was useful as well as my colleagues from Alberta and Nova Scotia who have been reelected, and they wanted those people to bring about some change. Well, we are still waiting for a renewal.
I can tell you something, and 1 will quote from official documents of the Government. Things were not that bad in Montreal. At that time, we did not hear about problems like we do now in Montreal, and 1 am very concerned because 1 am first and foremost a Canadian and a Montrealer. And I do not forget my Quebecker status, which means I am a good Que-becker-Montrealer-Canadian.
However, in a magazine called L'economie du Quebec 1984 published by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, one can read, and I will only quote one paragraph: "For the second year in a row, the rate of growth of the Quebec economy has been higher than the national average". The Conservatives were not yet in power, or had been for a very short time. "Thanks to the sustained growth of the manufacturing and trade sectors, the real gross domestic product has increased by 4.9 in 1984, that is half a percentage point more than the Canadian economy as a whole. The improvement of the economic situation also resulted in a decrease of the number of bankruptcies in all economic sectors, except the resource sector". Our good friend, the Minister of Public Works said exactly the same thing earlier and I quote: "Since we came to power 18 months ago, we ..." I was listening very carefully as 1 always do when our friend the Minister of Public Works is talking. Always, faithfully. I found that quotation in an official report, no less; entitled L'economie du Quebec 1984 published by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion of the Government of Canada. I have it in my hand so that people can see it. There are copies available. It was released in August 1985. At that time-
I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, what has changed since that time, and I am sorry to have to mention that. People tell me sometimes I should be a little tougher. Nevertheless I am sorry to have to say that, Mr. Speaker. In Montreal we need doctors, that is strong Ministers who are able to deal with problems when they arise.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we had problems in Montreal in the past, but the Ministers representing the island and the city of Montreal were so powerful that they immediately found solutions to them-and I will conclude with this hoping I will be asked some questions-what about Versatile, Vickers, Bombardier, Gulf, Canadian Steel Wheels and others; indeed,

we had problems in the past, but in those days we had people in the Cabinet who could give help to those important companies such as Vickers and Bombardier. But what do we see today? For all those 40 ridings in the Montreal region, I do not mention the Hon. Minister for Public Works who knows very well how to take care of his own area and riding-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. First, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member on the quite remarkable way he described what is going on in Quebec, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like him to complete the last comments he made in this House about the situation on Montreal Island, especially in the eastern part. What are the problems and what solutions can we expect in the future?

I would like to thank the Hon. Member. I shall be very brief because the rules say that we must be but it is really tragic, Mr. Speaker, that each time we ask the question to the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), she can only quote imposing figures. 1 can assure you that the workers at Versatile Vickers, Bombardier, Gulf, Canadian Steel Wheels, Parisette, D'Aoust & Lalonde, SKD Technology, of Montreal, and the others who will be joining them will not use these figures to buy food next Christmas or next Easter. They want jobs and they want the Government to act immediately. This is what is happening in Montreal East, and there is one thing I have noted for one of the first times in my political career. I went to Vickers, and in spite of what the Minister of Employment and Immigration said this morning in reply to one of my questions, we cannot sit on all the committees when there are only 40 of us and 21 legislative committees and 23 parliamentary committees. We know how to share work in my party and we have done so. We have the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi), the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) and the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre). We each deal with certain issues.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that these people, and especially the Vickers employees will not be satisfied with speeches or statistics, they want jobs. I know the Minister of Public Works very well, we all know he has a big heart, that is why I ask him to try and understand the desperate situation of Vickers employees. They thought they had an iron-clad contract and they see it go somewhere else. Even if it creates jobs elsewhere, it does not help them. I have met these people who will come on Parliament Hill and that is why I ask the Government to do something to deal with the sad situation in Montreal East,

November 8, 1985
Supply
because nothing creates more social problems than plant closures. If one closes, others are sure to follow .. . this is the domino effect. I know the Government is going to study the matter, but $100,000 to create a committee with the provincial Government, called Manpower Adjustment Committee, or MAC for short, will not solve the problem. 1 was at these meetings, Mr. Speaker, and I can tell you, and there is no doubt in my mind, that this people will not accept that we abandon Montreal East totally. You can ask my colleague from Bourassa, who was with me, or the Liberal Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano). They have met these people.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: A question from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle).

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) a question. Concerning the contract signed by the former Government, it was clearly stated in the original contract to St. John's that of the six frigates, three would be built in Quebec. If there is an oversight today, I think the Hon. Member will understand the problem and it is that Quebec and not necessarily Montreal was mentioned. I am sure this contract was not concluded in bad faith, since guarantees were sought. It is now difficult if not impossible to politicize the debate, because there will be no job loss in Quebec. I understand the frustration of the people in Montreal who are bound to lose those jobs to other workers in Quebec.
However as Quebecers, I do not think we will quarrel about jobs in Quebec. I think that the Minister who was then responsible forgot a comma, because Montreal is not specifically identified. I think that the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis will admit that oversight which is the cause of a major problem but we should insist on that matter.

Mr. Speaker, I have a short answer for the Hon. Minister. When that contract was awarded, it was understood that the Levis shipbuilders, near Quebec City, would have their share. Because they had lost that contract so to speak, they were given something else, that is the retrofitting, or TRUMP program, for $650 million. Montreal got the other contract. It is so obvious that that was the real intent of the Government, no matter what the legal contract says, that the people from Saint-John, New Brunswick, were forced to go to Montreal since Paramax was directly linked to that contract. Paramax, which creates some extraordinary high technology jobs is not in Quebec City but in Montreal, to stay closer to shipbuilders. Those are the facts that need to be remembered.
Therefore, I would submit to the Minister what I consider a shrewd proposal. If, as is your intention or not whether there was an error, the contract now goes from Montreal to Levis, I tell you in return, take the TRUMP contract from Levis and transfer it to Montreal. This would make sure that the people
concerned in east end Montreal and In Quebec City are happy, because the TRUMP contract was given to the people in Levis who were expecting the contract that went to Montreal. Do the reverse. But, please, do not let people out of work, please, Mr. Minister. I urge your Government not to allow those people to be out of work. This will be a disaster for them. They can no longer be displaced. You know very well that, with all the great programs of your colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. MacDonald), it is difficult to place people in other jobs at their age. The Minister knows this very well. Mr. Speaker, you are a reasonable, intelligent and understanding man, you know very well that those people who have just lost their jobs cannot be placed in other industries. And yourself, if you had to decide, you would find that so clever that you would say: This sure makes sense, the TRUMP contract was given to Levis, let us give it back to the Montreal people who just lost a contract to Levis. Clearly, this is so very obvious.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle), who spoke for some time about the advantages which the Government of Canada provided to the country, particularly to the Province of Quebec, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) said that those advantages came about because they were on stream from the previous Government.
Would he take this opportunity to explain to the House and to Canadians why a $200 billion debt, which takes one out of every three tax dollars to pay for the interest on that debt, is an advantage? Had the Government been left with a stronger economy, which had not been blown away by borrowing, we would have been able to do much more than the Hon. Member is now suggesting that we are. Can he not reflect upon his own past in that regard?

speechtext:

The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon).

Mr. Speaker, today the House is considering a motion presented by the New Democratic Party concerning the situation in Quebec. The motion reads as follows, and 1 quote:
That this House condemns the Government for abandoning the people of Quebec by reneging on its commitment to:
(1)	Develop new job potential in Quebec communities;
(2)	Ease the tax burden on low and middle income families; and
(3)	Protect and safeguard key existing industries such as lumber, textiles,
agriculture, pulp and paper and footwear.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to the third point which deals with the situation in Quebec's industry.
What is that situation? Mr. Speaker, today, if we consider all the statistics on the unemployment situation, we see that Quebec has an unemployment rate of 11.8 per cent. That is an increase over last month and constitutes a level of unemployment that is not acceptable in this country. However, some regions of Quebec have unemployment rates that are even higher. For instance, Jonquiere and Chicoutimi have an unemployment rate of 15.5 per cent. The city of Montreal has an unemployment rate of 11.4 per cent, far too high for a city of its size.
Mr. Speaker, if we look at regions in Quebec that are located far away from these urban areas, and I am thinking of the Gaspe-In the Gaspe, we find unemployment rates as high as 17.1 per cent, 40.6 per cent, 40.9 per cent. This is intolerable in our country.
And these problems are the result of a widespread loss of jobs in industry in Quebec.
I have here a list of all the jobs lost in Quebec after the Progressive Conservative Government was elected last year. There is for instance in Ormstown a textile industry where 80 jobs were lost. There is another small plant in Saint-Jerome where 30 people lost their jobs. The list could go on and on and on. There is for instance a small clothing factory where 55 people lost their jobs. But those are minor setbacks. There seems to have been a change this year in Quebec. Some shutdowns are taking place which create massive unemployment. Take for instance the case of Shawinigan with 175 jobs lost.
There are many other cases in such industries as lumber, footwear, leather, but mostly in the textile industry where losses are quite severe. Last May, for instance, in Quebec, 264 workers became unemployed at the Wabasso plant in Shawini-
Supply
gan and 560 at the Wabasso plant in Trois-Rivieres. Those are weak industries, small scale industries, but industries which used to play a major role in the province of Quebec. Today 1 wonder that the Government's strategy is in tackling the problem of those losses in the manufacturing sector of Quebec.
I believe there is no strategy, and I do not say that because I am a socialist, a Member of the NDP, I am saying it because I have discussed the matter with the textile industry in our country and they handed me their files and in the files you find a lot of interesting things.
In the files of the textile industry, for instance, you find a statement by the Conservative Party, a statement for immediate release, on July 26, 1984. That was close to the elections. This is the way they look at things in that statement: the Progressive Conservative Party will be committed, and it is a promise: first to fair trade, but not free trade.
That was not said by this NDP member. The Conservative Party said no to free trade before the election. It is true, that was your opinion.
Secondly, with respect to the textile industry. Stability is based on a promise of comprehensive quotas and a controlled increase of imports. Where is that promise now? There are no such comprehensive quotas. The Minister has perhaps forgotten them? Is that the explanation? I do not think so because the textile industry has held meetings with the new Tory Ministers who will provide a great future for Quebec.
For instance, in November 1984, the textile industry arranged for a meeting with the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) and responsible for international exchanges. At that meeting, the textile industry set forth all the problems and difficulties experienced by the textile sector in Quebec and referred to all the jobs which would be lost if nothing were done.
Mr. Speaker, what has been done? Nothing! The textile industry is quite articulate and thinks that the Government really wants to respond to the industry. After a year's work to arrange for another meeting with the same Minister, on October 4, to deal with the same matter, with the problems it was experiencing, the textile industry told the Minister: "We told you that if nothing was done many jobs would be lost in the textile sector. And now since you have done nothing, many, many jobs are lost".
And at that October meeting the Minister was asked if it was then possible to arrive at some decisions. Was it possible then to amend the textile industry policy in a way that would be consistent with their election promises? Was it possible to have comprehensive quotas? The Minister answered no, it was not possible.
I have before me a press release issued before the election, which says: Here are comprehensive quotas, they are for you too if you vote Progressive Conservative. But after the election,

November 8, 1985
Supply
the textile industry told me the Minister had said: No, that is not possible.
And the textile industry apparently was not the only one to have made that proposal.
I have here a letter from the Quebec Government which says exactly the same thing. This letter, Mr. Speaker, is signed by Rodrigue Biron, the Quebec Minister of Trade and Industry. It reads, and I quote:
The announced shutdown of the Dominion Textile Company plants in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu and Valleyfield, with the resulting layoff of more than 800 workers, and the recent Wabasso shutdown in Trois-Rivieres and Shawinigan, with the resulting loss of 1,000 jobs, are but a few examples of the disastrous situation facing the Quebec textile industry.
And this is not an NDP Minister but a Quebec Minister who sent the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, Mr. Sinclair Stevens, this letter last August to ask for the implementation of global quotas. It is a small, direct and simple request, related to a promise the Conservative Party made before the election, and it is something very important for the future of the textile industry in Quebec as well as in the rest of Canada.
Here is a communication from the committee for the survival of the textile and clothing industry, it is an invitation to join forces so that this great magician, the Canadian Government, will not make our industry vanish because imports are not restricted. The survival of the textile industry is now for sale. But what does the Government do? It does nothing. Mr. Speaker, this Government has no strategy at all. We see the same thing happening in many other areas, like forest products industry, clothing and textile industry, for which there is no strategy. There is a strategy that could support Quebec communities and inform them about their economic future and that of our country. Take the Desbiens situation for instance. This is a project our Party considers very important, Mr. Speaker. During our tour, we visited Jonquiere and found this small pulp and paper mill, and we have fought for Desbiens, asking in the House that the Government support this industry. It might not be a big struggle, but it is the struggle of a community which does not want to become a ghost town. This community seeks a balanced economy with jobs and a future.
When we raised questions, the Government announced help for Desbiens. But this now brings an other important question. The private company, which was considering building or renovating that small plant, has backed down. We must find an other solution and the House should take up this challenge. When we have this kind of small community which thinks in terms of planning the future, I believe we should have economic tools to help them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments. Debate. The Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin).

Mr. Speaker, first I must say that I am a little moved to be recognized after some very experienced members such as the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) who brought forward this motion, then the Hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle), of course, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) and last my colleague from the New Democratic Party.
Earlier today, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville proposed this motion in this National Week of Career Counselling announced by the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), 1 hope the hon. members of the NDP will take this opportunity to train for another career than prophet of doom in Quebec. I beleive this is a golden opportunity.
Moreover, I would like to indicate that the Hon. Member who is the sponsor of this non-confidence motion before us, said he belonged to a party which represents ordinary people. I, for one, as Member of Parliament for Charlevoix, I come from a region and I have not been elected by the previous Liberal "establishment" but precisely by ordinary people. I am the representative of a peripheral area. I represent ordinary people. I am Member of Parliament for a region where unemployment rate vary between 20 and 80 per cent. In my riding, I succeeded to a Liberal Minister, the Minister of Public Works, as well as Minister for Small Business and Tourism. When 1 was elected, I found that the economic situation in that riding was just as bad as everywhere else in Canada and particularly in Quebec.
I would like to say as well that I agree with the last intervention of the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) who spoke about the poor East Montreal region which is now in difficulty. I sympathize with those people and I suffer with them. But what about our peripheral areas, what about us people from the Upper North Shore, from remote areas like the Abitibi, from Gaspe, Riviere-du-Loup, Rimous-ki, who are constantly facing prohibitive transportation costs and business investment disincentives? I sympathize with people of East Montreal. I am quite sure that the meeting which is taking place between the Members from East Montreal and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) as well as some of her colleagues will bring about solutions. This is a unique opportunity for them, given the
November 8, 1985

closeness of markets and so on, to start a new process in East Montreal.
As for us, what has been done for us during the last fifty or hundred years? We live in outlying, isolated areas. It happens that 13 or 14 months ago we too in Charlevoix in particular and in Eastern Quebec generally, voted, with an overwhelming majority for change? Why did we vote Progressive Conservative?
Precisely because we wanted to breathe into our people, the disadvantaged, a new spirit, a will of change, a will to control our affairs.
The previous speaker was talking about a mere 11 per cent unemployment rate. If I had an unemployment rate of only 11 per cent in my riding, I would be taken for a god. People would kiss my hands and feet. I would be carried in triumph.
The fact is that unemployment in my area is well over the national average. We always exceed it. And we avoid comparisons, because although it may sometimes be comforting it can also be distressing at times. In the area of underemployment and underdevelopment, we still have much progress to make. Yet we have started making some progress in cooperation with people. For example, just a day ago, I was 60 miles deep in the forest as a result of a deal made with Miss MacDonald to invest $509,000 in a forest management project. I was in the ditches with the guys, about a hundred men working at forest management and feeling proud and happy, despite the temporary nature of this investment, to be able to control the future of the forests. Because, of course, Charlevoix is also the country where Le temps d une paix was filmed, it is the Little Switzerland of Quebec and indeed of Canada and one of the most beautiful areas of our country.
I urge my hon. friends to support the tourist industry in my riding by visiting Charlevoix next summer or even this coming winter . . . they could ski there also. That is an invitation. They will find excellent accommodation and can expect a warm welcome on the part of my constituents who are working hard to change things and improve their lot.
And I do my part too, as a backbencher, or rather, as I often tell the people in my area, I am a proud "front-sitting backbencher". We have managed, thanks to the Hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. MacDonald), to get some $15 million to invest this year in my riding and to mobilize my constituents around a number of projects which are a little more significant and around which we hope to create long and middle term jobs, for in spite of all the investment contraindication, we are trying to adapt to a changing situation. We make very effort to do so, Mr. Speaker.
The results are often late in coming. Like people in other areas, those who have lived for years up there on a Cadillac level find it hard now to step down to a Volkswagen. However, I urge them to follow the example of our people and to show
Supply
this new spirit. Along those 100 miles of coastline my riding is almost 300 miles long-there are communities with just one small industry and often during the winter, you can count on you left hand those who are working. Do not waste time counting those who do not work. It takes too much time, the other way is easier.
However, we are trying to rouse those communities and to breathe into them a new working or creative spirit. And 1 was quite pleased, indeed, to take advantage of the support provided by my Government for certain projects and that creative spirit is going quite far. One of our industries was advertising today in the Globe and Mail its intention of issuing a new series of shares once it will have secured a loan from the Quebec Government which has not yet been confirmed. However, in view of their worthwhile project, which is to build a fifth pulp and paper mill, those people are issuing new shares. And I can tell you that the decision to expand has come from within, from the workers, the ordinary people, the leaders and the unions who are fostering this development and asking for this new investment. I hope that the issuance of new shares will be really successful and that they will find the necessary capital without too much help from the Government. Of course, they have asked us to intervene. They asked the Quebec Government. If the Governments of Quebec and Canada had been willing to open up the valves, we would have been the first on to congratulate them and to provide financial aid to that business. However, what is more fantastic yet is that they have done it all by themselves encouraged by the worthiness of their project. I feel this is great and I hope it will result in the creation of 200 or 300 jobs in an area which is highly underprivileged, but still experiencing major technological changes.
Some investments have also been made under the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle). This week, a $800,000 project in my constituency will get under way for the refitting of a new wharf. The use that is made of those wharves will be changed. I have had funds invested this year in Tadoussac, where the tourist industry is experiencing new developments, where very low unemployment rates have been felt in that small community because of the natural phenomenon of whales visiting our shores. This is an extraordinary event, which year after year generates activity with people coming to enjoy that tremendous attraction. And this has been done by local people. There is a new spirit that is spilling over. And, of course, If we had all that money available, if it were not for that damned $200 billion deficit, if the previous Governments had not run wild with the coffers, we might afford to add to all this activity. There is also a tremendous awareness effort in the small community of Sacre-Coeur, where cooperative movements "rehabilitated" a mill. Yet, the previous Governments had spent $47 million, but because of the distances those $47 million proved to be unproductive investments. There were successive failures, but for the first time, the local people took
