over that investment and the company manager, assisted by the chairman of the cooperative union was proud to show us the 196,000 board-feet of average production, a figure never before achieved for that mill and which has steadily been maintained for some months now. That same cooperative union with others in the area, and even some private investments are triggering a process that will, as I wholeheartedly and despite unfavourable conditions, our remoteness, the financial reluctance of the banks-In remote areas like the North Shore, banks think that assets have no resale value at all whereas in Quebec City, you can get loans up to 70 per cent or 80 per cent of your investment, because banks know their money will easily be recovered if the project fails. The bank thinks: "I will recover as much as 70, 75 or even 90 per cent of my investment." In our outlying communities, you get 0 per cent. And investors must give iron-clad guarantees.
Despite all that, however, there exists a new climate, a new will and a new hope. And contrary to what today's motion implies, I think that we are creating new opportunities in the remote areas. If past debts were not so heavy we could build our future more rapidly.
Now, this is a young Government and despite a lack of resources, it stimulates people and investments. When my Government says it intends to negotiate free trade, it has a tremendous impact where I live. However, free trade is important for the forest industry, the lumber industry, the sawmills which cut our timber. Should the Americans decide to limit our exports, as they intend to do under the influence of the protectionist lobby responsible for the Gibbons Bill and others, something we watch very closely, it would be a disaster.
That is why it is crucial that or Government anticipate that trend and tell the Americans: "Let's sit down and negotiate". Naturally, our people expect our Government-elected for that purpose-to protect the interests of the average Canadian. 1 can tell the Hon. Members of the NDP that, in my riding, dealing with the lumber industry and exports to the U.S. is dealing with ordinary Cannadians.
I repeat, I represent ordinary people, not the Establishment.
I was working on a project in a community of 800 inhabitants. We had the financing. We had, thanks to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Department of Manpower and Immigration, the Government of Quebec and Hydro Quebec, a nice little project of $1.7 million. We were to announce it, to start creating 60 jobs, permanent jobs. But, the threat of American protectionism was enough to make the main developer back down. That was the only threat.
You can see the need for us to initiate such a process in the best interests of regions such as mine, where tourism and the forest industry, which often has low stocks because of the infestation by the spruce budworm, need investments. An agreement of $300 million has been signed with the Quebec
Government, and I have learned that workers in my constituency are already benefiting from this agreement. What is also interesting, is that-my colleague tells me that we should speak about remote areas, such as Pontiac, Gatineau, Labelle and Lac-Saint-Jean. He is right. This is Canada and Canada is a country of regions. If we were ever to forget that fact in Ottawa, this country could not survive. We, in the ordinary regions, are what make up this country.
As I was saying, this new agreement between Canada and Quebec is beginning to show results. There are new spruce trees in the forests and work for the unemployed in my region. It is unfortunate that this motion has been introduced by a Member from Saskatchewan, even though I have a lot of respect for him. I see his intervention as coming from someone who wants to invite us to do more for Quebecers. However, 1 can assure the Hon. Member that we, the new Conservative Members from Quebec, who might, it is true, not speak that often in this House... do you know what we are doing? We are waiting to see the results of all this experience.
Of course, we cannot judge the future by the past. We saw what our predecessors did. You, socialists, never had the opportunity to implement your proposals. However, the people in France now bitterly regret having done so, and there will be major changes in this regard.
However, I understand this proposal. I would rather view it as an invitation from a colleague to do more. But before redistributing wealth, we have to create it. We are now doing so with what little means we have at our disposal, but I hope that the policies we are implementing and which admittedly impose certain sacrifices on the public will enable the outlying regions to initiate an ongoing process to achieve their economic potential so that their needs will no longer always be subordinated to those of the major centres.
As for the 74,000 jobs created in Quebec, I would naturally have liked them all to be in Charlevoix. Some of them have probably been created in our region, and it is thanks to the dynamic attitude of this Government, to this new spirit of entrepreneurship, to this new will to promote development, because of which within four years, we shall have fulfilled our mandate to change, maybe not that much, but significantly, the economic picture in Quebec and Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member made a magnificent speech. We have many NDP members who could say the same, but we must say it is the same Government who decided to give away $865 million to two major banks. It is also the same Government which made cuts in RRAP, the program that was so helpful for your area.
I agree with what the Hon. Member had to say and it was very interesting to hear both speeches one after the other. I also think as a Member from a peripheral area, namely South Ontario instead of Quebec, but it is basically the same.
November 8, 1985

I think it is essential for all of us from remote areas to appeal to the Government who pays more attention to demands from Montreal, Toronto or Edmonton; we must tell him that he must now listen to remote areas.
I believe it is sound to struggle, it is important for the Hon. Member that we support him and we hope that during next Parliaments we will lead the Government to at last listen to what remote areas have to say. That would be helpful.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his support which, I hope, will be more forthcoming than in the past for this Government. I am as anxious as you are to achieve all these objectives and you know, I wish we would have the "Decade of remote areas", but we should give ourselves the means to achieve that end. My people and myself still have enough patience to understand that we must give ourselves the means to act, to give more consistency to this economy, to have more confidence in private enterprise because I too believe in it, even though it is difficult in our region. But I am prepared as well as my fellow citizens to ensure that we take some time, that we change our scale of values and that within a short time we may achieve all the objectives that this Government and this party... all the objectives I have set to myself as a Member of Parliament both for my riding and for all peripheral areas.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are over. Debate. The Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif).

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate, if 1 may, however, like my colleague I deplore the fact that the motion, which has my full support under these circumstances, has been introduced when most Quebec Members have to attend the Halifax convention. Be that as it may, I should like to take the next few minutes to voice my views with respect to the motion before the House.
As Hon. Members may recall, we were in the midst of an election campaign a year and a few months ago, facing men and women who were crisscrossing Quebec and making every kind of firm commitments. The underlying theme of all those commitments was "jobs, jobs, jobs". Everybody then knew the state of the country's financial situation. Canada's debt was not a secret to anyone and, more than that, during the months following the election of the present Government it became clear that our indebtedness was definitely not as outrageous as they had claimed throughout the election campaign.
It is therefore fair to say that they were fully aware of the Canadian economic situation when they made those hundreds of promises and commitments on the hustings. They knew that Canada had gone through extremely hard and difficult times when, unfortunately, the deficit was bound to increase. They knew what the score was all right, but it did not stop them from making formal promises. So election day came and we all know the results-the Canadian people gave a massive vote of confidence to the Progressive Conservative candidates.
Here we are now, November 8, wondering what has been accomplished during those short 14 months. We have been hearing all along that inflation went down and interest rates declined since they took office. We were also told that they had a strong mandate to take whatever action was necessary under the circumstances. Well, as everyone knows, one does not have to be an economist to realize that the current situation with respect to interest rates and inflation happens to be the outcome, the result which could have been generated only through policies which had been implemented long before the Conservatives even arrived on the scene.
They pass a number of measures. They introduce a number of bills, but the particular feature of this Government is that for the majority, if not for all of its initiatives this Government, dug into the pockets of the constituents of my hon. friend who are people of modest means, whose salaries are very small or very average.

November 8, 1985
Supply
There may be a certain logic in taking money from the people through direct and indirect taxation to lower down the deficit. On that basis that kind of rationale is acceptable. However, what is unacceptable, what is even odious, is the fact that these sums collected through taxes on drugs and deindexation of family allowances, are being given away to the tune of $1 billion or several hundred millions to individuals or companies which also have certain responsibilities under the circumstances and should participate in the economic recovery of this country. It is totally unacceptable to take money from people who cannot afford that extra expense.
Still under the theme of job creation, they also said to the people of the region I know best, the Eastern Townships, the Bois-Francs, that they were going to develop, as soon as possible, a number of projects, absolutely essential to the economy of the Eastern Townships to strenghten its infrastructure and to create direct jobs and thousands of indirect jobs.
Obviously, I am referring to map-making, to the gas pipeline which should have linked Sherbrooke, Windsor and Asbestos and would have created hundreds of jobs as a result of infrastructure improvement.
They also said, because this is an agricultural oriented region, that they would develop a project which had been announced in June, a research laboratory, the phytoprotection laboratory, in Victoriaville. The cost of that project was 12 or 13 million dollars. Agriculture Canada had given its approval. This amount of $12 million was to come from the Laprade Fund, but once again, the project was postponed indefinitely.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), in response to a question that I put to him last week, said that he did not know enough about the project to answer a question of this importance. These were issues with a regional dimension. These were issues which were and still are necessary, in order to preserve the basic and significant economic nature of the Eastern Townships and the Bois-francs.
But there were other issues as well. Personally, I come from an asbestos producing region. During the election campaign, it was said that asbestos was a very important natural resource and that we should intensify research activities in this field and make additional efforts to promote it again in order to be able, eventually to consider transforming that product in larger quantities. What happened to the asbestos? A year and a few months after September 4, some 1,200 layoffs in the asbestos sector were announced; 1,200 people who were very well paid, lost or will lose their jobs in the next few months and weeks; 1,200 direct jobs that will disappear. It is well known that jobs earning $25,000, $30,000, $35,000 or $40,000 per year are very contributive to the economy and themselves generate an enormous number of indirect jobs.
So, what happened in that regard? Nothing at all. Absolutely nothing. Yet, it would have been easy for Canada which professes to believe in asbestos to put into place policies that
would have served as a model, on the international level, to issue guidelines to all construction undertakings to use as many asbestos-based materials as possible. Asbestos is no longer the controversial substance it once was, and it can now be used in a scientifically acceptable fashion. There is evidence that asbestos can be useful, even protect and save lives. It just have to be used safely according to rules and regulations.
There have also been commitments concerning an industry that is of special interest to me, that has been the subject of a fight to which I have been closely associated and still is, that is the footwear industry. The footwear issue is very simple and easy to understand. There are 20,000 jobs in Canada in footwear manufacturing, equally distributed between Ontario and Quebec, 10,000 in each province. Approximately 100 million pairs of shoes are bought in Canada.
At the present time, we import about 65 million pairs. Some will say I am against imports. I am not opposed to imports, 1 am for a just and equitable share of the Canadian market for manufacturers, through protectionism, with a view to ensure half of the market that is estimated at 100 million pairs. If Canadian manufacturers were guaranteed that share of fifty per cent, Mr. Speaker, the 20,000 jobs would first be secured. Second, that would lead to the creation of 6,000 new jobs in the next few weeks or months, at most within a year. During the last election campaign, there were men and women representing the Party which is now the Government who came to Quebec and said: "If we are elected, we solemnly promise to continue the quota system. We will make sure the jobs in these vital industries for the Eastern Townships are fully protected." They made a clear commitment to maintain the quotas.
What has happened? Under pressure, the Government is saying that it is in the interest to the consumers to abolish the quotas. I feel it would be easy to prove the opposite, because importers are very much interested in getting rid of the goods manufactured in this country and replacing them with imports with a much greater profit margin. When they speak, these people generally do so on behalf of the retailers. Well, there are some 4,000 independent retailers in the footwear industry who are never consulted, who never have their say and who in fact are for the protection of the Canadian footwear industry.
The Government had clearly defined its stand during the election campaign. The quotas which had been established under the Liberal Government were coming to an end. As a matter of fact, they will effectively do so in November. The Government promised to make its decision known last August. Then, it promised to make it known in September. Then it said it would be in October, and although the date today is November 8, there is still no decision. And the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) stated today in the House that the Government would make its decision known before the end of November. At the end of November, a decision will be made concerning footwear, and quotas end November 30.
November 8, 1985

However, we must realize that the decision, even if it were a good one, and I did take notice of the statement of the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), namely that jobs would be safeguarded . . . Even if this decision is good at the end of November, some harm will have been done, a prejudice will have been done, for which we will have to pay next year, because as everyone knows orders in the footwear industry must be placed 6, 7 and 8 months in advance.
Now, importers, assuming that quotas would disappear, have already placed their orders; they have already made their purchases for next Spring and next Summer.
Now, even if the decision were good, some harm, a prejudice would have been done to the Canadian manufacturing sector. Why? Simply because we were passive, because we have not made a decision, because we have not delivered after making formal commitments which were very clear, very precise.
There is also the textile and clothing industry, although this is another sector. At the present time, we talk a lot about the necessity to turn to a free trade policy, about the necessity to liberalize trade with the United States. In a constituency like mine, and I am not the only one in this case, there are dozens in Canada, constituencies which would in fact become extremely vulnerable if the economic barriers, customs barriers, with the United States were to be abolished.
Dozens of small businesses which do not have the capacity to invest millions or even billions of dollars, are literally going to go bankrupt. Small businesses which employ presently 25, 30, 50 and 100 people and which, in the case of free trade without conditions, will disappear. Unfortunately a constituency like mine cannot hope to benefit from the investment of billions or hundreds of millions of dollars, considering that such investments are generally made in densely populated areas. Remote constituencies or those which are not too close to large centres will fall victim to the consequences of such a policy.
1 am proceeding rapidly because there is another fundamental aspect for Quebec which, in my opinion, has been totally and shamefully ignored, namely, agriculture.
And speaking of agriculture, the spokesperson for your political group, now the Hon. Roch La Salle, said in Lon-gueuil: To live you have to eat. We understand that. He was inferring that farmers would get everything they wanted under a Conservative Government. In a question I put to the Hon. Member I mentioned the $13 million they have been waiting for all this time. According to the Minister's comments, they can now forget the whole deal. You have adopted a Bill which according to some Members is fantastic for agriculture and I am referring to Bill C-25, the stabilization legislation. This is an unprecedented setback for Quebec farmers, and here, they all agree that they have been sold down the river by the Members from Quebec. Not a single Quebec Member rose in
Supply
the House or even expressed disapproval of this measure which was an insult to everyone involved in agriculture in the province of Quebec. Today, those same farmers are very concerned about the Government's indecision-it reminds me a little of the footwear industry-about establishing a long-term dairy policy. It has been promised repeatedly by the Government, which was very emphatic about it, even implying that production costs would cover all the input, all the elements involved. We are still waiting. It was promised for August 1. The Minister has said time and time again: You will get a longterm dairy policy and we are going to release it on August 1. Today, on November 8, we still have no policy. They are now talking about reviewing a problem which had aroused considerable interest, and I am referring to the Crow rate. They are considering the possibility of putting that back on the table, with the clear implication that eventually, payments will be made to the producers instead of to the railways. Most farmers in Quebec are very pessimistic today about this whole issue.
Still on the subject of agriculture, Mr. Speaker, and with your permission, since we are often given this opportunity, I would like to talk about what the agricultural or the agri-food industry has been discussing in recent weeks in a journal which comes very close to what the Government's official spokesperson on Agriculture Canada, the Parliamentary Secretary, was saying: We are not here to play Santa Claus, and the Government is no longer financing the shortfall between production prices and costs. We cannot apply social welfare or social insurance policies to agriculture. That is what he had to say about the stabilization bill. A little later, that same Parliamentary Secretary, the same official spokesman of your Government said: I was feeling somewhat uneasy as I spoke in favour of Bill C-25, but I do not feel I am a traitor ... Because the word traitor is not used by him, but by the farm community which says that the Quebec deputation is composed of 59 traitors, and these will be my final words, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my Hon. colleague indeed for allowing me to qualify somewhat this aspect, which seems important in the circumstances, since that argumenta-

November 8, 1985

tion has been cropping up repeatedly on the other side of the House, namely that we too in the past were somewhat unfair to the people benefiting from social programs, which by the way had been introduced by the Liberals. The 6 and 5 per cent were not aimed just at the lowest income people, they applied to every sector of society, every individual and every company. The basic feature was that the first 6 per cent were unassailable, sacrosanct, and that the restrictive measures, if any, applied to the higher amount. The policy put forth by this Government concerns the first 3 per cent, and this means people will lose the first, the second and the third percentage points. Now within that context, the decision reached by the previous Government under the 6 and 5 policy which this Government is taking advantage of because if we are so often told today that the inflation rate is good, that growth is on again, it is the result of measures such as those taken by the Liberal Government. The 3 per cent are not aimed at large companies, at the rich people, at those who will benefit from capital gains of $400,000 to $500,000, but at the people to whom my colleague was referring, the little people who really need those 3 per cent.
I agree, as I said earlier in this House, that 50 cents, $1, $1.50, $3, $4, $5 per month are not much, but people are vulnerable. But what 1 say is that for these people, it is very important to know one, two, three months in advance that they will have $5, $10, $15, or $20 to spend on Christmas. It is these people who suffer the most because of your unfair measures. And what is even more despicable is that you are literally bleeding them to feed big companies, very big companies that do not need that money at all.

Mr. Speaker, the Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) has raised quite an interesting point. He talked about asbestos. According to him, asbestos is not as dangerous today as it used to be because of new processes. Will he explain which processes he is referring to when he says that as such asbestos is not hazardous to health?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know of a Member who could give some of the details, I think, and I mean my colleague because I understand he is from Sherbrooke. And in the Sherbrooke area, asbestos is most important. What I want to say is this: at a time asbestos was submitted to a lot more research than any other resource, product or commodity. We had an unbelievable volume of expertise on it and I do not think there is anything on the Canadian market that has been subjected to that many studies and analyses. Obviously, when a subject is as researched as this one has been, it is difficult not to find some failings. But what I am saying is the properties of asbestos have been identified as well as the effects of a non-regulated use, in other words, we know all about the parameters involved in the use of asbestos. And since we fully
know about all the peculiarities of this natural resource, asbestos can now be used in a totally safe way.
Finally, I will say, Mr. Speaker, that dynamite, gasoline and a lot of products that are extremely more hazardous than asbestos are being regularly transported-we realized and accepted that those are essential products to the same extent as asbestos. Furthermore, asbestos has saved and is still saving hundreds of lives.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to take this opportunity to thank my colleagues for their contributions, and especially my colleague for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin). If there was any need for an example of involvement by Conservative Members, I think he has set it. The Hon. Member for Charlevoix has been an advocate of regions, and has been promoting his own region within that spirit of renewal that motivated all Quebecers and all Canadians in 1984. He has realized that it is not by handing out money to a region that it will become a dynamic region.
The work required now from those Members who want to respect the movement they set up, who want to respect the people is indeed to get involved, to work very hard and to motivate their community. The Hon. Member mentioned a current example in his area, a business which has decided to invest although it has no definite feelings that there will be government involvement.
That determination to invest is to be found also in the Charlevoix region; it is to be found throughout Quebec, throughout Canada.
Those who are monitoring the situation, and 1 do not mean the Government or any political party, but people who usually monitor the Canadian economy ... we have had over these last few weeks the economic statements of the Royal Bank of Canada. If you take a close look, all indicators are positive. The average number of hours worked in manufacturing industry is growing, the house building industry is picking up and so on. The Royal Bank of Canada has good news; a real economic recovery is taking place in Quebec.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business talks as well about a steady growth in employment and capital investments for small businesses. It indicates that the capital gains exemption announced in the May budget has clearly brought about stronger investments. That is yet another analysis confirming that we are achieving our objectives and that better days lie ahead for the Canadian population.
The Canadian Economic Council is also optimistic. Canadians can well have faith in the economy of their country. There is indeed a recovery and this recovery will continue.
November 8, 1985

A moment ago, my colleague from Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) was mentioning among other things the regional unemployment situation. The Hon. Member from Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) said that the unemployment rate had just gone up slightly. To better make his point, he stated that this rate is unacceptably high for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that anybody speaking about unemployment in this Chamber would always find the rate unacceptable. Any unemployment is wrong, and the Government's task in this regard is precisely to find remedies.
If you look abroad, you will see that the current OECD forecasts put Canada right behind Japan. I must say I feel very good being placed there by OECD in terms of economic growth. If that growth can be allowed to continue, Canadians will have a more stable and more balanced standard of living.
Cost of living increases are presently stabilised at around 3 or 4 per cent. Deficit for the first five months of the year is only $300 millions. Compared to last year, this is already an improvement.
All these improvements, and my friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) touched on that this morning, could in part be attributed to the spirit of cooperation. We have the will to succeed, but this will must be supported by a better understanding between the various levels of Government, general acceptance by the population and cooperation at all levels.
Within a year, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion supported 559 projects in Quebec which will generate some $648 million of investment. They will create 12,324 new jobs and help maintain 9,400 others. Naturally, there are problems in certain areas or certain industries. What we must avoid is tranferring the problems, that is to say solve the problem of an area at the expense of another. We have to be more dynamic, more innovative and we must find new solutions.
I heard a lot about federal-provincial agreements. They too mean money spent in Quebec, for the Quebec people. A moment ago, my friend, the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (M. Hamelin), was talking about the benefits for his area of the forestry agreement.
There are also other agreements which will have an impact in Quebec in the areas of industrial and regional development, and tourism. These total over $450 million. If we look at industrial development, under the agreements already signed, $152 million have been committed, of which 50 per cent will come from the Federal Government. We have therefore put aside $77 million to help certain businesses in Quebec.
As concerns tourism, $32 million have been allocated. We could also add the amount of $45 million already allocated under federal-provincial agreements by the Government since its coming to power.
Under all regional and industrial development programs, $90 million were allocated between September 1984 and April 1985, and another amount of $22 million has been allocated since April.
Supply
The Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe said earlier that we have done nothing for the textile industry. We should not forget that this Government is now working on a textile policy which will be proposed and developed in consultation with the industry, and that, this year, the Canadian Government has allocated an additional amount of $44.4 million to the textile industry through the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board. In the textile, clothing and shoe industries, 234 projects have been approved which made it possible to create or preserve 1,730 jobs.
There is another program developed by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion to increase the productivity of the defence equipment industry, under which $95 million were provided to Quebec manufacturers between September 1984 and April 1985, and $31 million since April.
We must not forget either that the Federal Government provided an amount of $10 million to help the Quebec Labour Federation create a small solidarity fund. Such contributions could be offered to similar organizations on the condition that they were created in accordance with provincial legislation. This is another contribution to the Quebec economy.
The Hon. Member, whose constituents probably go to the various financial institutions to ask for loans, should know that, this year, the Government has taken care of small businesses and, under the Small Businesses Loans Act, it has guaranteed 11,524 loans to small businesses for a total of $342 million.
The Federal Business Development Bank has granted 938 direct loans since September 1984, which represents an investment of $220 million.
Quebec businesses now owe $457 million to the FBDB. When we look at these figures, it is impossible not to realize that this Government wants to allow our businesses to become more dynamic. If the Government-During my own electoral campaign, I insisted on two major themes, which were also the two major concerns of the people in my constituency, in Quebec and throughout Canada, namely unemployment and the economy.
If there is one thing that my constituents understood, it is that it was impossible to lower unemployment and improve our social programs if we did not succeed in promoting economic recovery. What this Government and private businesses can do at the present time is to continue to work together. It seems easier to increase the deficit to stimulate the economy than to try to work with local businesses and people to have them take control of the situation and invest in the economy in our areas. I appreciated very much the comments of my colleague from Charlevoix because he seems to understand that it would take more than grants to get his area moving.

Mr. Speaker, I do agree with my colleague that some of the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) were very interesting and attractive. What I want to know is what do you say to those who need this Government effort in the area of resources when, on the one hand you give billions of dollars to large corporations and on
the other you tell them: "Listen, we do like the idea, the initiative, but, as you know, the country's financial situation does nos allow us to get involved in your investment?"
What can you tell them after having invested billions of dollars with the multinationals? As a sub-question, I understand that there is a footwear industry in my colleague's riding; what do you tell those workers? That you did not make the decision? What do you tell them, considering the simply disastrous impact of the present situation? And a final question, with your permission. My colleague has access to data that could certainly have been interesting to this House if she had told us what proportion of her Department's funds has been spent in Quebec as opposed to those spent elsewhere. It would have been interesting to have those figures.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to admit I am not too sure about the meaning of first part of the question about the billions of dollars we could not promise the multinationals, but still I will try to answer as best as I can.
Obviously projects submitted cannot all be considered, for various reasons. Therefore some projects get our support while others do not, and my colleague should know that, as a rule, the preference will go to cases which will produce results, and we would rather not provide help when no jobs are created. So we will set priorities and respect them.
My colleague referred as well to the shoe industry. Mr. Speaker, I am quite interested in that file. 1 have been working on it for quite some time, perhaps even longer than my colleague. You may think that you have a major problem in Richmond-Wolfe, but I should point out that in Charlesbourg we have 1,000 jobs directly related to the shoe manufacturing industry. There is no easy answer to that problem, and 1 would suggest that a parliamentarian who has been here for many years should know that different viewpoints are expressed in the course of negotiations, that it does take a little time to reach a consensus. As my colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) said, the shoe manufacturing industry should have an answer before the end of this month.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to take the floor and support the motion of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). I would like to respond to the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif) who said something about the money spent by the Government to help the shoe industry. She said that she was concerned about the fact that thousands of people would be losing their job in the footwear industry, in his town, but she forgets to talk about the commitment that her leader made, on May 4th, 1984, when he promised to maintain import quotas. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said then: "A Conservative Government would not abolish the import quotas in the footwear and textile industries".
November 8, 1985

On Wednesday, the Conservative Leader, Mr. Brian Mul-roney, pointed out to the newspaper La Tribune that the policy on quotas would remain the same, and he made clear that he was not in favour of free trade in these industries. He also added he did not intend to bow to the pressures that could be exercised by the Common Market on the United States in order to bring down the quotas on footwear and textile products in Canada. He said that he would not hesitate telling that to President Reagan, when he meets him in Washington, next month.
Mr. Speaker, they said that they intended to renew these import quotas at the end of the month. It was necessary to do it in September or October. Mr. Speaker, in September and October 2,000 may have been lost jobs in Quebec alone. Three hundred and twenty jobs were lost at the G.A. Corbeil Company, in Montreal. At the Empress Company, in Montreal, 100 workers lost their jobs. The companies Saint-George Shoe, in Saint-Georges de Beauce, Jean E. Blais, in Saint-Cezaire, Chaussures M.G., in Actonville, Boot Legger Incorporated, in Montreal, M. Lalonde, in Montreal, Popular Shoes, in Con-trecoeur, La Parisette, in Montreal and Gen Foot, in Con-trecoeur, laid off respectively 225, 110, 155, 375, 100, 147, 160 and 200 workers. In Grand Mere 100 jobs were lost.
Mr. Speaker, if the Government does not give its word, to maintain the import quotas on shoes, we could lose even more jobs, because Canadian retailers refuse to order shoes made in Canada, while waiting for the end of import quotas, this month.

I do not have very much time because I have to catch a plane, Mr. Speaker, but I want to make one more point in this connection. The public opinion on this point has been tested by a Decima poll which has shown that 44 per cent of Canadians consider imports are a serious threat to Canadian jobs and 66 per cent said that they would prefer to maintain quotas in order to protect jobs even if it means paying higher prices for footwear.
It is not enough to talk about all the great things the Government would like to do if it had more money or even about the things the Government may have done in subsidizing certain industries. The point is to renew the quotas on the importations of footwear, otherwise we stand to lose a whole industry in Canada of 20,000 jobs, as has been pointed out, half in Quebec and half in Ontario. That is the action that is needed and it is not a substitute for that to give certain subsidies or to promise certain grand programs for the future. If those companies give up because they are losing the Canadian market to countries that pay wages perhaps one-tenth of ours, then it will be too late to try to restore the industry by government subsidies. I would urge the Hon. Member for Charles-bourg (Mrs. Tardif) to consider this and to use her influence

with the Government to have those quotas declared and restored immediately.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House will allow me to raise another point before dealing with the motion proper.
Today, I should like to congratulate a former Member of the House who last Sunday was fortunate enough to be elected Mayor of the City of Verdun.
Mr. Raymond Savard was elected Mayor of the City of Verdun, and I take this opportunity to assure the new administration of my full support and cooperation for the next four years.
Mr. Speaker, I should like now to turn to the censure motion which the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has moved and where he condemns in part the Government for abandoning the people of Quebec by reneging on its commitments. As a Quebecer eager to defend the rights of my province and region, I can hardly accept that.
When he says that the Government has failed to develop new job potential in various communities, 1 point out that the Verdun-Saint-Paul riding which is not much industrialized has managed to create over 900 jobs last year. The Government

November 8, 1985

has invested $1 million in my riding to create these jobs, and it would be very difficult to demonstrate that Canadians are unhappy or dissatified with the efforts their elected members have made in their respective ridings. It is a fact that many industries are faced with problems. But there is a whole new generation of politicians who have entered politics to improve the well-being of the people and provide them with better services, to make it possible for them to work at something they like and raise the living standards of their families, and I think they will achieve that in a not too distant future.
Admittedly the textile and footwear industries are in a very difficult position now. i have had the opportunity of travelling and meeting with many people who export their products in Canada. Here, we are told that we do not protect our industries; and yet, when we go to other countries where footwear and textiles are produced, we are simply told that our industries are overprotected, that the market is completely closed, that the exporters are not allowed to sell their products on the Canadian markets. One must understand that our textile and footwear industries are indeed in a very difficult position, where the markets are invaded by virtually all the countries of the world.
There is also the fact that these people have an expertise in various types of machinery, and they have the know-how; and I am confident, for the Montreal area for example, that very soon there will be an economic upturn, an upturn which will bring new industries and high technology. I believe that we must mention it, because all over the world, Canada has the reputation of being an unequalled producer of high technology. I am confident that very soon we will be able to retrain these people who will have lost their job; it is indeed true: in some industries, we will retrain the workers in other fields where we do have state of the art high technology on the international level.
We must also recognize that the new programs, the housing programs, will create many jobs. They will put to work many people. 1 will give again the example of my area, the riding of Verdun-Saint-Paul.
Last year, I managed to get more than 235 housing units that were subsidized by the federal Government. This meant that people were needed to build and improve and repair them. And when people say that we are not doing our best to reduce the tax burden on families, especially on low income families, and I am not saying that my riding is any poorer than another riding, but these are average people who work hard to succeed and who have worked hard to get what they have today. And now, thanks to these subsidies and the jobs we are providing, these people will be able to live a better life, have a roof over their heads and a home that can compare with homes anywhere in Canada, and all this at very reasonable cost.
These people can live comfortably, can live very well and can prove to themselves that they have the respect of all
Canadians, that no one can tell them they are poor and they have to live in poverty, because that is just not true that some people want to be poor or think they are poor and will never get ahead. When I decided to go into politics, I had thought about it for a long time. Several years ago, I decided 1 wanted to get involved in politics and do something for the people around me, and I ran in the municipal election. I found this an extraordinary experience, because now I had a chance to meet people in their own homes, to see what their needs were and find out where they worked and what they did and what they had against the system. But I realized that at a given level, one cannot do more.
A new team was formed at that time, a team with an extraordinary leader, someone who believed in Canadians and who was prepared to give all Canadians a chance to succeed, to achieve their goals and stop being jealous of others.
The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) gave me a chance to become a member of this team when he said quite simply: "I am giving you a riding, but it is not an easy one." These people have been manipulated for years and years and told time and time again that with a Conservative Government, they would not get anywhere and would lose everything they had. However, at 30, and 1 was actually 29 at the time, all this was a challenge, and you do something because you believe in it. I really took the bull by the horns and I went to see these people who did not belong to my municipality at the time, they were living next door. These people had always been told: "Oh, we don't care about the people of Verdun because they are poor." Nobody was interested and nobody wanted to get involved. But today, 1 am proud to say the people of Verdun have understood.
Those people gave me a chance to go and meet them, speak to them, and stop telling them lies and telling them consistant-ly that everything was going to be taken away from them, that they were not going to be allowed to succeed, they were not going to be given a chance, because the Progressive Conservative Party was the Party of the rich. The last elections showed a participation by those people. The percentage of votes went up by 15 per cent from 60 per cent to 75 per cent. So there was indeed a dissatisfaction among them.
The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) was wrong, I believe, when he said earlier that we no longer study La Fontaine's fables at school. I, for one, have been lucky and fortunate enough to have parents that allowed me to learn, to study and to travel. And what I have learned is what I want to give to the people of my constituency of Verdun-Saint-Paul. Day after day, they come and see me. It is not true that they always come and ask for jobs, and tell me that they are unhappy, that things are not going well, that they pay to much tax, that their pension is about to be cut, that they are not satisfied with Bill C-70 on family allowances, and they do not want to have it. All that is not true.
November 8, 1985

Many express very hard views, but we let them speak. As you know, being a Member of Parliament today no longer means that you just work five days a week. It does not consist simply in attending functions and cutting ribbons. It means being in your office and meeting people who come and tell you about their everyday life, tell you about the difficulties in the plant where they make shoes; tell you that the Unions are sometimes much too harsh with the bosses or with themselves. You have to go and meet those people at home. You have to speak to them.
And when I see a Party like the New Democratic Party, to me, the New Democratic Party are socialists. How could we accept a socialist Government in a country like Canada? Canada is a country of free enterprise where everyone is allowed to succeed. And if someone is rich, it means that he has worked and has been successful, and has been involved in an environment, in a community. It should be clear that if I personally spend hours and hours working, I shall never ever accept overnight to give everything I have to people who don't want to do anything. An I am not afraid of saying that to anyone. When people come and see me at my office and tell me: "I am willing to work, but I want to work 35 hours a week with a salary of $40,000 a year", I ask them questions. For instance, I ask them: What is your educational background? What can you do? And frequently the same answers crop up. Eight year. They gave up and are frequently what we call dropouts. I am willing to help them, but not by taking money out of the taxpayers' pockets. It would be most unfortunate for the people of Canada and mostly for that particular individual, because I fail to see what interest there would be for that individual to live off the government.
The Conservative Party really had new ideas to offer and it proved it by bringing new Members to the House and when 1 say "new Members", 1 do not mean only young ones, from 27 to 35 years of age, but also new Members who are 50, 60 or 65, as well as socially involved women, not only the feminist type who have a grudge against males, but also women who are willing to work in the community, for the prosperity of their constituents and neighbours. Our Prime Minister gave us that opportunity.
Now, they try to tell us that we are not keeping our promises in Quebec when we work late every night, seven days a week. The NDP Members are not the only ones to work late at night. We do too every day, seven days a week, in order to give our constituents the service they are entitled to receive and that they did not get for a number of years.
How is it that everywhere we go people keep asking us: How come you are not treated as a VIP? You are the Hon. Member of Parliament and you should be seated at the table of honour and be asked to make a nice speech about all of the Government's achievements. In fact, most Conservative Members go to see the people, sit with them and discuss their problems. We listen. We are not members of Cabinet. It is

very difficult to change decisions once they are made, but at least there are Ministers who listen and give us a chance to say what we have to say. However we do not give them our personal views but those of thousands of Canadian men and women.
If sometimes we reverse a decision like the one on the deindexation of pensions, it is not because we fear the electorate. On the contrary, I think that our Prime Minister is too smart to waste his time on polls. It is because each and every one of us went in our constituencies to talk to our senior citizens, who told us that they were against it for numerous reasons. We had the opportunity to express those reasons to the Cabinet, to the Right Hon. Prime Minister, and the decision was made there, at a time when every Hon. Member had the opportunity to express his views. This is democracy. This is what I call enabling people to make progress ina country all of us can be proud of.
Could some people say that they are not proud to live in Canada? How many of us have travelled all over the world to see poverty in other countries? We say that there are no jobs here: have you been in France, have you seen what the socialist party has done in France? I have a personal example. My family has been in business for years, for more than 40 years, and we deal with a French company which had been in business for 130 years. Because of the socialist government, because of unions which really twisted its arms and prevented it from working, that company will close its doors and lay off 250 workers this year. Strangely enough, people here want a socialist Government thinking that the Government will give everything, whereas we have blatant examples in various countries. For us in Quebec it is easier to find examples in France, because we are much better informed on France, particularly because of the language. Do not deceive our people, the Canadian people, in believing that your ideas are better. Tell them the truth, tell them that Canada is the ideal country, the place where young or old people, where any one who has an idea can succeed if he wants to work. There is no free lunch.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) is not trying to do to his leader what the Liberals have been trying to do to theirs since September 4.

Mr. Speaker, in closing the debate on this motion today we have to be aware that this is a national Parliament. The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has quite correctly and appropriately drawn our attention to a number of national problems and their adverse effects in the Province of Quebec such as the lack of effective job-creation programs. There is an

November 8, 1985
Supply
inequitable tax system which causes low and middle-income families to pay more than their fair share of taxes in Canada, and difficulties and problems in certain industries or sectors such as the forest products industry. These are all national problems with serious effects in Quebec as well as in other provinces.
It does not matter to what extent the Government boasts about job-creation endeavours. As Members of Parliament we still have to face up to the fact that we have double-digit unemployment in Canada, much higher than in the United States. Everyone I think rejoiced rather cautiously when the unemployment rate in September dipped to 10.1 per cent. It has not been at that level for a long while. Everyone hoped that this was the beginning of a new trend, but when the figures came out today, as we begin to approach another long and probably cold winter, we see the unemployment rate is once again building upward. In October there was an increase of .2 per cent so we are back again to 10.3 per cent. Now there is concern that this may be a trend that is going to be with us for several months. It is most disturbing that in these figures there is an increase of .6 per cent, taking us to 8.5 per cent unemployment for young men in this country between the ages of 15 and 25. The unemployment rate among women in the same age category is also alarmingly high, nearly 14 per cent. In Quebec the unemployment rate is above the national average. It is nearly 12 per cent, compared to 10.3 per cent for the rest of the country. In Atlantic Canada we learned from questions in the House today that the situation is really in a state of crisis. Prince Edward Island in one month had an increase of 1.8 per cent in unemployment, taking that province over the 13 per cent point. New Brunswick had an increase of 1.5 per cent in a single month, increasing the rate of unemployment to 15 per cent. In Nova Scotia it is 13 per cent, and in Newfoundland it remains at almost 20 per cent.
I can well understand that a Government wants to boast about job creation and quote figures about the number of jobs created in a certain period of time. However, I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was correct and apt when he stated this morning that he took no satisfaction at all from these statistics. I think all Members of Parliament share that feeling with him.
The United Church of Canada, Mr. Speaker, has a national working group on the economy and poverty. It met with a Liberal caucus task force last summer. It used some rather strong language in talking about the May 23 Budget. It referred to that Budget as being obscene.
You should have heard what they said about the MacEachen Budget.
The Budget the Hon. Member is bellowing about does not have any effect on Canadians today.
It sure does.

The Wilson Budget does have adverse effects. I do not know about the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) but I am living in the present. He wants to live in the past, that is his choice.
However, this working group condemned the Conservative Budget for one reason. It put the rich ahead of the poor and the unemployed. It gives tax breaks to the rich while at the same time it cuts services to the young. It cuts services to women and elderly and unemployed. Look at the figures that this working group provided for us. It pointed out that no matter how well we think we are doing in this country in our attempts to alleviate poverty, there is still one in five Canadians classified as poor. Some 75 per cent of this nation's wealth at the top end is held by 10 per cent of the people. At the bottom end 1 per cent of the wealth is held by 40 per cent of the people. Realizing that, one wonders how the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) could bring in the kind of Budget we heard on May 23.
In the same submission the Church told the caucus quite clearly that the situation is getting worse. I am among those Members of Parliament who feel a deep sense of concern about the size of our deficit. I am concerned about the growth in our national debt. However, at the same time, I cannot help but be aware that in 1945, at the end of World War II, on a per capita basis we had a higher deficit than we have today. Despite that we managed to live with it. Not only that, successive Liberal Governments were able to bring in a number of social programs which today are part of the very fabric of our society, programs which the Prime Minister during the election campaign described as a sacred trust. Social programs will not be part of the negotiations when we deal with the United States on a free trade agreement, said the Government.
Our focus today really ought not to be on reducing our social programs. That is not where the emphasis should be. That is not where we should be looking for better accountability and better use of scarce financial resources. We ought to be looking at the elimination of government mismanagement and waste. Cutting social programs at the very same time we introduce legislation in this House which will cost the taxpayers nearly $1 billion to pay unknown and uninsured depositors in two failed banks is extremely difficult for my constituents to comprehend. I cannot explain it to them and I share their perplexity. We do have an inequitable tax system in this country, as suggested by the motion in the name of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville. However, when you add together tax revenues lost on personal income which escapes taxation, to that of corporate write-offs, there is enough money there, about $31 billion, to cover our federal deficit.
I wanted to take some time to speak about the third item in today's Motion, namely problems with the forest industry. However, suffice it to say in the time remaining that the forest industry is in some difficulty at the present time. I am at somewhat of a loss to understand or appreciate exactly what the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) in this Government is doing. He promised last April that he was going to carry on extensive consultations with interested Canadians regarding the forest products industry. We have yet

to hear from him. It is now November. What has he learned from these consultations? When can we except him to announce a national forest products strategy to help overcome some of the serious problems we are facing? There is the problem of protectionism in the U.S., especially with reference to softwood lumber; the instability of domestic and foreign markets; the need for an effective reforestation program. Like other Members of Parliament, we are wondering, debating, asking questions about the free trade agreement to be negotiated with the U.S. At present, Sir, we have free trade with the U.S. in lumber. There are many people wondering if any new comprehensive free trade agreement, while it may on the one hand remove the threat of congressional legislation which

would have the effect of limiting lumber exports to the U.S., on the other hand are wondering if a free trade agreement is not also going to lead rather quickly to some kind of parity between our currencies. If that were to happen, and it probably will, along with the effect of declining interest rates, 1 suggest it will be far more serious for our lumber exports than any quotas imposed upon us would be.
